u1s1: Security seals are tamper-evident mechanisms that seal valuable material in a room, cabinet, vehicle, or other storage facility.
u2s1: Such seals can help to detect theft or contamination, either accidental or deliberate.
u3s1: Security seals are commonly used to secure truck trailers, vessel containers, chemical drums, airline duty-free trolleys, keys and utility meters.
u4s1: == Vulnerabilities == Security seals are not designed to resolve all security problems: The effectiveness of seals is strongly dependent on the proper protocols for using them.
u5s1: These protocols are the official and unofficial procedures used for seal procurement, storage, record keeping, installation, inspection, removal, disposal, reporting, interpreting findings, and training.
u6s1: With a good protocol, a modest seal can provide excellent security.
u7s1: On the other hand, a sophisticated seal used poorly may be worse than useless if naively trusted.
u8s1: The same organization demonstrated that a trained individual was able, using low-tech methods, to defeat 90% of the 244 seals they studied in less than 3 minutes, and all of them in less than 44 minutes.
u9s1: They offer ideas on countermeasures, and are exploring the promising option of "anti-evidence" seals.
u10s1: == Operation == Security seals can be split into two main groups: single-use and reusable.
u11s1: Single-use seals are typically made of plastic or metal, and the used material and production technology is the key to their security level.
u12s1: Reusable seals are usually electronic or mechanical rather than just made from plastic, and if purely plastic, only one part is reusable.
u13s1: Electronic and mechanical seals are generally used for the transportation industry, with seal fixed to the back of trucks, trailers, and shipping containers.
u14s1: A reusable mechanical or electronic seal can be fitted to the rear or loading doors, extending a cable from itself through fixing points on the doors, and when sealed generating a unique number which is logged.
u15s1: === High Security Seals === A High Security Seal is constructed and manufactured of material such as metal or metal cable with the intent to delay intrusion and have been designed to conform with world customs and ISO security seal standards.
u16s1: A measure of a seal's security is whether it has obtained an ISO 17712:2013 rating.
u17s1: US Customs-Trade Partnership Against Terrorism (C-TPAT) and the World Customs Organization's Framework of standards, endorsed and encouraged the use of ISO compliant seals.
u18s1: The requirements for certain security level of seals are defined in the ISO 17712.
u19s1: The seals that belong to the High security level and Security level are also called "barrier seals".
u20s1: Cable seals and bolt seals also fall into this category.
u21s1: The seals that are in the Indicative level as to ISO 17712 are made of plastic or thin metal.
u22s1: === (HMRC) Customs Accepted Seals === Customs accepted seals are security seals which the customs department of a given country will accept as a secure seal to be placed onto a container.
u23s1: This does not mean that all exporters or importers should place a customs accepted seal on their containers or trailers.
u24s1: Many businesses who transport high value goods like to use Customs Accepted Seals as these seals have been through rigorous testing and are of high quality.
u25s1: The UK Security Seal Testing Authority tests these seals on various points such as "Tensile Strength", "Effects of Heat", "Direct Effects of Freezing", "Effective Numbering & Marking", "Tamper Evidence", and more. UK Customs Accepted seals are sorted into three various categories, Group 1 consists of seals which withstand a force of 1000 kg, Group 2 consists of seals which withstand a force of 250 kg and Group 3 consists of other accepted seals.
u26s1: View all UK customs accepted seals here.
u27s1: == Metal seals == There are several basic designs of the metal seals; bolt seals, ball seals, and cable seals.
u28s1: Bolt seals are used to secure shipping containers, trucks, and trailers.
u29s1: A bolt seal used for securing containers must conform to the ISO 17712 high security seal in order to be accepted by customs all around the world in ocean shipping.
u30s1: The C-TPAT (Customs Trade Partnership Against Terrorism) specifies ISO 17712 compliant security seals to be used.
u31s1: Bolt seals are generally closed by hand (by pushing the seal body and head together) and opened with the use of bolt cutters.
u32s1: This gives a strong and secure seal for transportation, while remaining convenient for staff in ports and warehouses.
u33s1: === Cable seals === Cable seals allow for more versatile application, as they have variable length of the locking mechanism limited only by the cable length.
u34s1: Most cable seals are classified as security or high security level as to ISO 17712.
u35s1: All ISO 17712 compliant seals are numbered on both seal body and head, to prevent substitution of either part.
u36s1: Ball seals are commonly used for securing trucks.
u37s1: Most ball type seals belong only to the indicative level as to ISO 17712.
u38s1: == Plastic seals == Plastic security seals are manufactured normally in two styles; adjustable or fixed-length.
u39s1: Adjustable-length seals can fit many applications from securing the neck of a bag or mail sack to sealing chemical drums, first aid kits, and fire extinguishers.
u40s1: They have an adjustable length much like a cable seal but offer a much higher security level and an audit trail due to sequential numbering and the ability on some seals to be bar-coded and have a company name and logo printed or laser etched on. Fixed-length seals tend to be more tamper resistant than variable-length as there are no sliding parts, they simply "click" into place to lock, which can make them easier to fit than variable-length seals.
u41s1: Most fixed-length seals can also be branded and numbered for extra security.
u42s1: Fixed-length is often the choice of single-use security seals for transport applications.
u43s1: Padlock seals are usually supplied as a completely plastic seal, shaped as a standard padlock would be.
u44s1: Technically, they can be classed as a fixed-length seal.
u45s1: The most common use for these seals is for airline duty-free trolleys.
u46s1: Meter seals are used with electric or gas or water meters and usually molded in polycarbonate.
u47s1: The transparent body of the seal means that the locking mechanism is visible, and can provide clear indication of tampering.
u48s1: Meter seals can withstand exposure to sunlight and extreme weather, and a wide range of temperatures.
u49s1: Some meter seals contain components which glow under ultraviolet light, allowing the seal to be easily located in darkness.
u50s1: == Technologies for marking the seals == The seals can be individualized to fit the needs of the user.
